newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan strikers offer to meet with president.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan strikers offer to meet with president.

text.p: Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega on Wednesday said he was willing to meet Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman in a bid to resolve a three-day national strike.

Ortega told a news conference that international mediation was needed for the negotiations to end the strike, in which pro-Sandinista protesters have set up barricades, burned tires and blocked off some highways since Monday.
"I'm willing to converse with him to lay a basis for a dialogue...to overcome this crisis. A dialogue that allows us to reach an agreement that gives stability to this country," he said.
Aleman on Tuesday proposed a meeting with Ortega, who was Nicaragua's president from 1984 to 1990, but he rejected international mediation to end the crisis.
Prior to Ortega's offer for a meeting, Aleman said in a live television broadcast that the government had decided to order anti-riot police to clear blockaded highways.
He said peaceful protest would be allowed but demonstrators could not impede traffic. He did not say when anti-riot police would start clearing blockades.

While the strike's affect on the capital has been minimal, protesters have blocked traffic on some highways outside Managua, especially on a southern stretch of the Panamerican highway, where a long line of cargo-laden trucks had formed, state radio reported.
Business leaders said the strike's effect on business so far had been minimal, but could increase if the strike lasted much longer.

"Their strategy is to strangle Managua, but the trucks have been getting through the barricades. So far it has not had a large impact on sellers," said Nicolas Garcia Baltodano, general manager of the Mercado Mayoreo, Nicaragua's largest grains, fruits and vegetables market.
Garcia told Reuters that 90 percent of the supply trucks were arriving at the market, but there could be shortages if the road blockages lasted nine to 10 days more.
Police said about 5,000 protesters have set up at least 25 barricades across Nicaragua, and late on Tuesday hooded gunmen burned a bus that was operating in spite of the strike call.

Strikers are protesting the government's economic policies, which they say are pushing people out of work. They also want legal titles to confiscated property received during the Sandinista land reform.
